strengths: Identifies a clear and useful insight: conversion of open-set detectors (e.g., Grounding DINO) to centroid predictors is a key driver of recent detection-based counting performance, and builds a strong, well-motivated baseline (GDino improved) from this insight that alone is competitive with prior SOTA.

Proposes a conceptually clean and well-motivated contrastive learning method (C-REX) that operates entirely in image-embedding space rather than image-text space, avoiding known instabilities of cross-modal contrastive learning and enabling many more negative samples per anchor.

The modification to the supervised contrastive loss (restricting anchors to only positive samples, Eq. 4) is simple, clearly justified, and shown via ablation (Table 4) to provide a meaningful, consistent improvement over both the baseline and the unmodified supervised contrastive loss.

Strong, consistent quantitative results on REC-8K across MAE, RMSE, and F1 on both validation and test splits, with substantial margins over the only other REC-specific method (GroundingREC) and over strong class-agnostic counting baselines (CountGD, GDino).

Reasonably thorough ablations: contribution of the modified loss, number of selected positives N, and decomposition of baseline components (feature fusion vs. detection core vs. CL module), which helps isolate where gains come from.

Good qualitative analysis, including breakdowns by object count range and by referring-expression attribute category (action, location, orientation, etc.), plus supplementary failure-case analysis that is candid about limitations (e.g., text-based fine-grained attributes like specific bottle-cap markings, complex spatial disambiguation with birds on cables).
The extension to class-agnostic counting is a nice demonstration of generality of the framework, even though gains there are more modest, and this is reported honestly.
weaknesses: Evaluation for the core REC contribution relies on a single benchmark (REC-8K); given this is the only REC dataset in existence per the paper, this is somewhat unavoidable, but it does limit generalizability claims to a single data distribution/annotation style.

The claimed generality/versatility of C-REX is only partly supported: on CARPK (Table 3), the simpler GDino-improved baseline actually outperforms the full C-REX model, undercutting the narrative that the contrastive module is broadly beneficial across tasks; the paper acknowledges this but does not analyze why the contrastive addition hurts here.

The pseudo-labeling scheme for positives (top-N most similar tokens to the masked referring expression, using ground-truth count N as supervision) is a heuristic that could introduce label noise, particularly in cluttered/high-count scenes; the paper only partially validates this (claiming ~80% precision of selected pseudo-positives) without deeper analysis of its sensitivity or failure modes beyond N selection ablation.

Comparisons in Table 1/2 draw baseline numbers from prior papers rather than uniformly re-running all baselines under the authors' own protocol (except CountGD), which is a minor but real threat to strict comparability.

The technical novelty is somewhat incremental — it is largely an adaptation of supervised contrastive loss (Khosla et al.) to an existing detection-based counting pipeline (Grounding DINO/GroundingREC) with a targeted loss modification, rather than a fundamentally new architecture or paradigm; the primary innovation is the choice to contrast in image space and restrict anchors to positives.
No analysis of computational overhead/training cost introduced by the contrastive loss and larger negative pool, which would be useful for assessing practical trade-offs.

Limitations and failure cases (Figures 6–7 in supplementary) are informative but somewhat brief; a more systematic error analysis (e.g., how performance degrades with expression complexity or clutter) would strengthen the paper's completeness.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and underexplored problem (REC) with a clear conceptual contribution: performing supervised contrastive learning purely in image space (avoiding image-text misalignment) and exploiting ground-truth counts as pseudo-labels to select positives/negatives.

The proposed modification of the supervised contrastive loss (restricting anchors to positive samples only) is simple, well motivated theoretically, and empirically validated through a clean ablation (Table 4) showing consistent gains over both the baseline and the unmodified supervised contrastive loss.

Strong empirical results on REC-8K: C-REX clearly outperforms the only prior REC-specific method (GroundingREC) as well as the authors' own improved detection baseline across MAE, RMSE, and F1 on both validation and test sets, with the F1 metric explicitly guarding against the false-positive/negative cancellation issue common in counting metrics.

The analysis identifying object-centroid prediction (vs. bounding-box regression) as the key factor behind recent detection-based counting successes is a useful and generalizable insight, and the resulting 'GDino improved' baseline is a nontrivial, competitive contribution in its own right (near state of the art even without the contrastive module).

Good breadth of evaluation: results are reported not only on REC-8K but also on class-agnostic counting benchmarks (FSC-147, CARPK), demonstrating that the framework generalizes beyond its original task, with reasonable competitive performance in the class-agnostic setting.

Multiple ablations (loss formulation, number of positive selections, removal of baseline components) increase confidence in the design choices, and qualitative figures (main paper and supplementary) with both successful and failure cases add transparency and support the paper's specific claims about disambiguating spatial/attribute-based referring expressions.
Code availability is stated, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Evaluation for the core REC contribution relies on a single benchmark (REC-8K) with only one directly comparable prior REC-specific method (GroundingREC); broader validation (e.g., additional REC-style datasets or human-verified subsets) would strengthen the generality claim.

On CARPK, the plain improved Grounding DINO baseline (without the contrastive module) actually outperforms C-REX, which is a somewhat counterintuitive result for a paper centered on the value of the contrastive loss; the discussion of this result is fairly brief and could be expanded to clarify when/why the contrastive module helps versus hurts.

The number-of-positive-selections choice (using N = ground-truth count) is empirically justified (Table 5) but relies on having access to ground-truth counts at training time as a proxy label; the sensitivity analysis is somewhat narrow (only a few alternative strategies tested), and the approach's dependence on accurate N could be discussed more thoroughly, e.g. robustness to noisy/estimated counts at inference or partial supervision settings.

No variance/multiple-run statistics are reported for the main comparisons, and there is limited discussion of computational cost/training overhead of the contrastive module relative to the baseline, which would help assess practicality.

The technical novelty is somewhat incremental — it largely combines existing ingredients (supervised contrastive loss, Grounding DINO centroid conversion, pseudo-label assignment via top-N similarity) rather than introducing fundamentally new mechanisms; this is acceptable given the strong empirical validation, but the paper could better delineate what is conceptually new versus adapted from prior art (e.g., SupCon, GroundingREC, CountGD).

strengths: The proposed image-space supervised contrastive loss is simple, architecture-agnostic, and is validated as a plug-in across three distinct REC backbones (GroundingREC, CAD-GD, GroundingDINO) and two visual backbones (Swin-T/B), demonstrating broad applicability without architectural changes.

The paper provides a reasonably thorough ablation study (positive-selection strategy via bipartite matching vs. thresholding, the modified supervised contrastive objective vs. vanilla SupCon, and combination vs. replacement of image-text and image-space losses), which helps isolate the source of gains.

The extension to class-agnostic counting on FSC-147 shows the idea generalizes beyond REC, and the additional comparison against a modern VLM (Molmo2) and paraphrase-robustness experiments add useful context about the difficulty of the task and the practical value of specialized architectures.

The paper includes honest reporting of failure cases in the supplementary material, showing that C-REX does not always fix incorrect RE grounding, which is a meaningful and appreciated limitation disclosure.

The writing clearly motivates the problem (image-text misalignment, limited negative pool) and the method description, loss formulation, and rationale for excluding negative-negative attraction are clearly presented.
weaknesses: The core technical idea (supervised contrastive learning entirely in visual embedding space, using in-image tokens as positives/negatives) is a fairly direct adaptation of well-established ideas from SupCon, ReID, and dense/pixel-contrastive segmentation literature; the paper's own related work section acknowledges this, which somewhat limits the claimed originality to an REC-specific engineering adaptation.

Reported improvements are not uniformly positive: in Table 1, CAD-GD† with C-REX is sometimes worse than the baseline (e.g., Swin-T validation MAE 4.65→4.70 and RMSE 12.87→13.78), and in Table 5a the CAD-GD baseline outperforms its C-REX counterpart on paraphrase robustness, which undercuts the generality claim.

The FSC-147 class-agnostic counting results are mixed: GroundingREC+C-REX improves MAE/RMSE on the validation set but has a notably worse test MAE (10.12→12.46), which is not discussed in the text despite being a departure from the paper's general narrative of consistent gains.

The headline abstract claim of "up to 28% in MAE and 24.5% in RMSE" appears to reflect a best-case configuration (GroundingDINO+Swin-T) rather than a representative average across the many reported settings, which risks overstating the general magnitude of improvement.

The central motivating claim—that image-text embedding misalignment specifically causes the baselines' errors—is argued qualitatively (via illustrative figures) rather than empirically verified with direct evidence such as embedding-space visualizations (e.g., t-SNE) or alignment/entanglement metrics comparing baseline vs. C-REX representations.

There is no analysis of computational/memory overhead of computing the contrastive loss over hundreds of visual tokens per image, which would be relevant for practical adoption given the method's core motivation is scaling negatives.

Reproducibility for CAD-GD relies on the authors' own retraining since no official checkpoint exists, and while this is disclosed, it introduces a potential confound when comparing baseline vs. C-REX numbers for that model relative to the officially released GroundingREC checkpoint.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated core idea: shifting contrastive supervision for REC from a poorly-aligned image-text embedding space to a purely visual embedding space, addressing a concrete limitation (few negative REs, alignment noise) of prior work.

Strong generality/versatility demonstration: the proposed loss is applied as a drop-in replacement across three distinct REC architectures (GroundingREC, CAD-GD, GroundingDINO-based baseline) and two backbones (Swin-T/B), with mostly consistent gains in MAE/RMSE/F1.

Thorough ablation studies: comparison of image-text vs image-space vs combined losses, positive-selection strategy (bipartite matching vs similarity-based thresholds), and the modified supervised contrastive objective (positives-only anchors), each supporting specific design choices.

Additional generality is shown by extending the method to class-agnostic counting (FSC-147), and useful supplementary analyses such as robustness to paraphrased referring expressions and comparison with an off-the-shelf foundation VLM (Molmo2-4B), the latter reinforcing the continued need for specialized counting architectures.
The paper is transparent about limitations, including a dedicated qualitative failure-case analysis showing that improved counts do not always reflect correct RE-following.
Clear writing and figures effectively illustrate the core intuition (Fig. 1-2) and the practical benefits (Fig. 3-4).
weaknesses: Results are not uniformly positive: some configurations show C-REX underperforming the baseline (e.g., CAD-GD† Swin-B validation RMSE, CAD-GD under paraphrased REs in Table 5a, GroundingREC test MAE in the class-agnostic setting in Table 2), and these regressions are not deeply analyzed or explained beyond brief remarks.

The technical novelty is somewhat incremental: the core mechanism (supervised contrastive loss with bipartite-matched positives/negatives restricted to positive anchors) largely repurposes existing supervised contrastive learning (Khosla et al.) and ideas from ReID-style intra-batch contrastive learning, applied to a new task rather than introducing a fundamentally new algorithmic component.

No analysis of computational/training overhead introduced by the contrastive loss (e.g., additional training time, memory, or sensitivity to number of tokens/negatives), which would be useful given the method is proposed as a general plug-in.

Limited discussion of hyperparameter sensitivity (e.g., temperature τ, thresholding for CAD-GD†) and no reported variance across multiple runs/seeds, making it hard to assess the statistical robustness of the reported improvements.

The claim of state-of-the-art performance is accurate for REC-8K but the class-agnostic counting gains are explicitly and correctly framed as modest/expected, and in one case (GroundingREC test set) the method actually degrades performance, slightly undercutting the 'improves any counting model' framing in the abstract/intro.
